summary:
Project Orbital Equilibrium (ASTRO-SYS) is an interactive, data-driven Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) simulator designed to test cognitive load during orbital crises. We developed a gamified web application that integrates concepts from live NASA APIs (DONKI, OSDR, RadLab) and CSA lunar habitat data. The simulator forces users to balance four critically interlinked resources—Power (kW), Oxygen (kPa), Thermal Shields (K), and Bio-Systems (kg)—under a strict mathematical trade-off matrix where boosting one system inherently degrades another.

It addresses the challenge of making complex aerospace engineering accessible by translating static telemetry into a high-stakes, pressure-driven experience, complete with dynamic "Drain Multipliers" and an integrated ECLSS Verification Protocol.

This project is highly important because it bridges the gap between theoretical research and practical decision-making. It provides a low-cost, scientifically grounded training environment that enhances human readiness, teaches resource sustainability, and inspires the next generation of engineers to design resilient habitats for long-duration deep-space missions.
details:
1. What does it do or how does it work? Orbital Equilibrium (ASTRO-SYS) is an interactive, data-driven Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) simulator. It immerses users in deep-space emergency management by pulling real-time concepts from NASA APIs (including DONKI for space weather, OSDR, and RadLab) and CSA Lunar Habitat data. The simulator forces users to balance four critically interlinked resources—Power (120 kW), Oxygen (101.3 kPa), Thermal Shields (295 K), and Bio-Systems (500 kg). When a crisis occurs, users must make complex engineering trade-offs where boosting one system inherently degrades another. The application employs a dynamic "Drain Multiplier" to simulate compounding environmental degradation and features an integrated "ECLSS Verification Protocol" to test the user's comprehension of complex system interdependencies.

2. What benefits does it have? & What is the intended impact? The primary benefit of Orbital Equilibrium is its ability to translate dense, complex space agency datasets into a highly accessible, gamified cognitive stress test. It provides aerospace students and enthusiasts with a practical environment to understand the "Trade-off Principle" in closed-loop life support systems. The intended impact is to enhance human readiness and systems engineering education. By actively forcing users to manage resources against scientifically accurate parameters and real-world hazard models, the project inspires the next generation of engineers to design more resilient habitats for long-duration lunar and Martian missions.

3. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use? The simulator was built entirely as a responsive web application using HTML5, CSS3 (Tailwind CSS), and Vanilla JavaScript. For data architecture, we integrated live concepts from NASA Open APIs (DONKI, OSDR, RadLab) and referenced the CSA Lunar Habitat documentation to ground our crisis scenarios in reality. The application is hosted using standard cloud deployment tools. Additionally, we responsibly utilized Super Intelligence (SI) tools for rapid ideation, refining the mathematical escalation logic (the drain multipliers), conceptualizing the UI layout, and debugging the JavaScript simulation loops.

4. How is your project creative? Orbital Equilibrium is highly creative because it transforms static telemetry and research papers into an emotionally engaging, high-stakes experience. Instead of simply reading a graph about a solar flare, the user feels its direct impact as their thermal shields fail and their Power reserves plummet. The integration of interactive "NASA & CSA Brief Flip-Cards" alongside an active Engineering Verification Quiz seamlessly blends thrilling gameplay with rigorous academic education, ensuring that the user learns the actual science behind their survival decisions.

5. What factors did your team consider? Our team prioritized the delicate balance between strict scientific accuracy and engaging user experience (UX). We carefully researched real-world ECLSS dependencies to ensure our trade-off matrix used realistic units (kW, kPa, kg) and logical outcomes. We factored in cognitive psychology by designing a UI that intentionally induces a sense of urgency and cognitive load, reflecting the reality of mission control under pressure. Finally, we ensured the educational components were unobtrusive yet highly effective, integrating post-decision logs and quizzes to reinforce the learning objectives without breaking the immersion.
